artifactEvidence.excerpt: A front-end voice layer is the part that listens and speaks while a separate backend checks information and completes tasks. OpenAI calls listening and speaking at the same time full duplex. GPT-Live-1 can keep listening when a caller pauses, interrupts or changes direction. A separate backend system still checks business information, applies rules and uses tools. OpenAI’s documentation says the application—not the voice model—owns permissions, confirmations and the lasting record of a task.

Compared with a traditional voice system that passes speech through separate listening, reasoning and speaking stages, GPT-Live-1 is meant to keep the conversation moving more naturally. Imagine changing a reservation from four people to five while the voice is still replying. The voice layer can handle the interruption; the restaurant’s availability data and booking tool still determine whether a table is recorded.

explainBack.question: Why can a GPT-Live-1 call sound perfectly smooth and agreeable, yet my table for five still not exist when I arrive?
explainBack.answer: Because two separate systems are at work. GPT-Live-1 is only the front-end voice layer: it listens and speaks simultaneously (full duplex), so it handles your interruption when you change four to five. But it does not check availability or write anything down. A separate backend application queries the restaurant's data, applies its rules and uses the booking tool—and per OpenAI's documentation, that application, not the voice, owns confirmations and the lasting record. If the backend never writes the updated booking, the voice's fluent agreement changes nothing, which is why you repeat date, time and party size and ask for the confirmation.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must name the voice/backend split, full duplex as a conversational capability only, the application's ownership of confirmations and durable records (P004), and the resulting end-of-call check (P008).
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; nothing had to be imported from outside the text.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A caller phones a dental office whose scheduling line uses a similar voice AI. Mid-call she says: actually, make it Thursday at 3 instead of Tuesday, and add a cleaning to the exam. The voice smoothly says: of course, Thursday at 3 with a cleaning. Two weeks later the practice's system shows Tuesday, exam only.
unseenTransfer.question: Using only this article's mechanism, what likely happened and what should the caller have done before hanging up?
unseenTransfer.answer: The full-duplex voice layer handled the mid-sentence change conversationally, but the backend scheduling application either never received or never wrote the revised request; the voice does not own the durable record, so its verbal agreement is not the appointment. The caller should have repeated the final details—Thursday, 3 p.m., exam plus cleaning—and asked the system to read back its confirmed record, requesting a person if it could not.
